query: Which scalable GP approximations (inducing points, sparse variational GP, KISS-GP/structured kernel interpolation, low-rank) offer the best time/memory trade-offs for WSI-scale priors and at what patch counts do we switch?

response.query: Which scalable GP approximations (inducing points, sparse variational GP, KISS-GP/structured kernel interpolation, low-rank) offer the best time/memory trade-offs for WSI-scale priors and at what patch counts do we switch?
response.answer: Low-rank approximations and sparse variational GPs offer the best time/memory trade-offs for WSI-scale priors; switch to low-rank methods at around 10,000 data points.

results.title: Review of Recent Advances in Gaussian Process Regression Methods
results.content: Gaussian process (GP) methods have been widely studied recently, especially for large-scale systems with big data and even more extreme cases when data is sparse. This paper reviews the recently developed key factorised GP methods such as the hierarchical off-diagonal low-rank approximation methods and GP with Kronecker structures. Keywords: Gaussian process, factorisation, covariance matrix, hierarchical off-diagonal matrix, low-rank approximation. The first strategy sets a subset of training data or inducing points to construct a low-rank approximation to the GP covariance matrix with a smaller kernel matrix in size  [3, 4]. Instead of selecting the inducing points, the other strategy uses the low-rank approximation methods, which are based on the spectrum of the covariance matrix to remove the uncorrelated entries in covariance matrix [5, 6]. Specifically, after a short review of GP regression in Section 2, Section 3 reviews the classic inducing point-based approximation methods. Section 4 contains the Kronecker and Toeplitz-based structured approximation and the structured kernel interpolation (SKI) GP methods. The hierarchical off-diagonal low-rank (HODLR) matrix-based approximation method, which improves GPs in terms of scalability and capability, is reviewed in Section 5. The GP prior is decomposed as the sum of a low-rank approximation using inducing points and a full-rank residual process. Adam [14] proposes an improvement inference method for 1-dimensional input space to combine the advantages of both sparse GP approximation and state-space model representation, which results in a novel representation of inducing features as the state space components. The inducing point-based approach combined with a sparse approximation is popular since it can be applied outside the data set without requiring any knowledge of its structure. Besides the inducing point-based methods, another GP method based on the HODLR structure proposed in [6] has shown a very strong potential to solve the large data. Instead of the block-box inducing point model, the low-rank approximation gives a reasonable approximation based on the spectrum of the covariance matrix. The SKI and the HODLR with the Cholesky factorisation Gaussian process (HCFGP) method are slower than other inducing point-based methods due to the time taken for the interpolation and construction of the special matrices. This paper presents recently developed global sparse GP methods, including the classic inducing point-based, structured approximation and new HODLR-based methods.

results.title: Online variational Gaussian process for time series data | Journal of Big Data | Full Text
results.content: Unlike traditional methods that rely on a fixed number of inducing points, OLVGP adaptively adjusts the number of inducing points as new data arrives and optimizes them from the model, ensuring that the model remains computationally efficient while maintaining high predictive accuracy. The sparse variational Gaussian process approach has become the most important methodology in GP approximation, providing an approximation of the marginal likelihood that allows both the hyperparameters and inducing inputs to be learned from the data through gradient-based optimization. An adaptive method for selecting the number of inducing points is proposed, allowing the model to dynamically adjust its complexity in response to the coming data, optimizing the balance between computational efficiency and prediction accuracy. Over the past two decades, significant advancements have been made in developing sparse Gaussian Process (GP) models to overcome the computational limitations inherent in traditional GPs. The cubic time complexity *O*(*N*3) for training has driven research towards more scalable solutions, particularly through low-rank approximations of the kernel's covariance matrix [33]. While several frameworks and approaches have been proposed for dynamically choosing inducing points in variational Gaussian processes, significant challenges remain in the context of time-series data. Arguably, the most prominent probabilistic approximation involves recasting the GP as an exact model with an approximate prior, using *M* pseudo-points (also called inducing points, support points, or active sets) to summarize the original *N* samples, a technique known as sparse Gaussian Process (SGP) [55:1939–59.")]. While the approximate generative model framework offers several attractive advantages, optimizing the gradient with respect to the entire set of inducing inputs **Z** introduces an additional \(M\times d\) parameters, turning the inference into a high-dimensional optimization problem with a complexity of \(\mathcal{O}\left(dN{M}^{2}\right)\), where *d* is the dimension of the input space. The model learned at current time step contains the appropriate number of inducing points *M**b*, the optimized inducing inputs \({\mathbf{Z}}\_{\mathbf{b}}^{\*}\) and all the hyperparameters \({{\varvec{\theta}}}\_{\mathbf{b}}^{\boldsymbol{\*}}=\left\{{\sigma }\_{n}^{2},{\sigma }\_{f}^{2},{{\ell}}\_{1},\dots ,{{\ell}}\_{p}\right\}\), where we incorporate the noise \({\sigma }\_{n}^{2}\) into the kernel hyperparametersFootnote 9 for notation conciseness. Additionally, our algorithm dynamically determines the number of inducing points, adjusting the model complexity in real time based on the data, thus optimizing computational efficiency.

results.title: [2505.18526] Scalable Gaussian Processes with Low-Rank Deep Kernel Decomposition
results.content: # Title:Scalable Gaussian Processes with Low-Rank Deep Kernel Decomposition. Authors:Yunqin Zhu, Henry Shaowu Yuchi, Yao Xie. View a PDF of the paper titled Scalable Gaussian Processes with Low-Rank Deep Kernel Decomposition, by Yunqin Zhu and 2 other authors. > Abstract:Kernels are key to encoding prior beliefs and data structures in Gaussian process (GP) models. The design of expressive and scalable kernels has garnered significant research attention. Deep kernel learning enhances kernel flexibility by feeding inputs through a neural network before applying a standard parametric form. However, this approach remains limited by the choice of base kernels, inherits high inference costs, and often demands sparse approximations. Drawing on Mercer's theorem, we introduce a fully data-driven, scalable deep kernel representation where a neural network directly represents a low-rank kernel through a small set of basis functions. This construction enables highly efficient exact GP inference in linear time and memory without invoking inducing points. It also supports scalable mini-batch training based on a principled variational inference framework. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the advantages of our deep kernel GP in terms of predictive accuracy, uncertainty quantification, and computational efficiency. ## Access Paper:.
